mcqs.question: The dataset in this area puts Python in 70.8% of 6,964 AI postings (78.8% of AI Engineer postings in Spain). A hiring manager reads that as 'the service must be written in Python'. Which reading of the number does the data support?
options: It measures the language the job is written in day to day, so shipping a TypeScript service would contradict the requirement in most ads.
It measures how often Python appears because it runs the model faster, which is why the ad asks for it ahead of other runtimes.
It counts a keyword in job ads, and the keyword follows the Python-first SDKs: the model tooling layer needs Python, the service language stays a choice.
It measures demand for research engineers rather than service engineers, so it is the production postings that ask for TypeScript.
mcqs.explanation: The figure is a keyword count in job ads, and the ad asks for Python because the model and evaluation libraries ship there first: the tooling layer is Python, the service layer is a choice, which is why the plan treats Python as the depth track and still keeps a TypeScript variant. The strongest distractor is the first: it turns a mention rate into a description of the codebase, and a 70.8% mention rate says nothing about which process in the system runs Python. The second misplaces the runtime - the model runs at the provider, not inside your service, so speed is not the mechanism behind the number - and the fourth splits the dataset into research and production roles, a split the posting set does not make.

mcqs.question: A 90-minute pair session hands you an existing service and one ticket: a provider 503 must stop surfacing as an unhandled 500. The interviewer watches you work. What is being measured?
options: How you would have designed the service from scratch, since the ticket is only a vehicle for the architecture conversation.
Recall of the framework's API: decorators, dependency injection and which Pydantic major version is current.
Algorithmic fluency under time pressure, because the pair session doubles as the coding screen.
Reading code you did not write, changing it without breaking its contracts, and proving the failure path with a test.
mcqs.explanation: The gate is comprehension and safe modification: the bank's wording is working in the codebase without mentally translating it to another language, and the ticket forces exactly that - find the call site, read the existing error mapping, change one branch without breaking the endpoint's contract, then show the failure path is covered. The strongest distractor is the greenfield one, because candidates prepare design and want to display it, but rewriting the service in the session discards the constraints the ticket is about, which is the opposite of the measured skill. API recall is what a docs quiz measures, and the algorithmic option assumes a LeetCode screen: the ticket is deliberately small, and small tasks are what expose reading and testing habits rather than puzzle speed.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks what happens when you fan out 200 model calls with one `threading.Thread` per call, each waiting around 2 s on the provider. Which answer shows the depth being probed?
options: The waits overlap and a waiting thread is nearly free, so 200 threads is well within what an OS handles comfortably.
The waits overlap because a blocked socket releases the GIL, but 200 live threads still cost stacks and context switches.
The GIL serialises the calls, so 200 threads take 200 x 2 s in sequence; only a process pool can overlap a network wait.
The waits overlap, and so does the parsing: with 200 threads the JSON post-processing runs in parallel across cores.
mcqs.explanation: A thread blocked on a socket releases the GIL, and that release is the whole reason threads hide I/O: the interpreter keeps running other threads while the socket waits. What the GIL does prevent is two threads executing Python bytecode at the same time, so the 2 s waits overlap and the parsing does not - which is also the error in the fourth option. The real cost of the 200-thread version is per-thread: stack memory and OS scheduling, which is why asyncio is the cheaper default for I/O fan-out and why the first option's 'nearly free' is the wrong side of that same trade. The strongest distractor is the third: it applies the bytecode rule to a blocked socket, where the GIL is not held at all, and concludes that threads cannot overlap I/O - the opposite of what the interpreter does.

mcqs.question: This endpoint passes the demo. When the provider returns 503 for 40 minutes, every `/answer` request stays open until the load balancer cuts it at 60 s, and the provider's dashboard shows the key retrying thousands of times a minute. The body is `while True:` around one `await client.post(MODEL_URL, ...)`, returning on 200 and looping on every other status, with no attempt counter and no delay. Which change fixes it without redesigning the endpoint?
options: Keep the loop and give each attempt a 20-second timeout: once an attempt can fail, the loop drains and the request ends.
Pass the provider's 503 through unchanged so the client sees the real status, and stop validating the body on non-200 answers.
Move the loop into `asyncio.to_thread` so the retries stop starving the event loop, and keep the retry policy as it is.
Cap the attempts, retry only 429 and 5xx with backoff and jitter, and answer 502/504 with a typed body: one bounded call per request.
mcqs.explanation: The loop has no attempt count and no status policy, so a 400 from a malformed request, a 401 from a rotated key and a 503 from an incident all become the same hot loop: the thousands of calls per minute and the 60-second hang are one defect seen from two sides. The strongest distractor is the first, because it sounds like the missing piece: a timeout bounds each attempt, not the number of attempts, so `while True` at 20 s per attempt still never ends, it just reports nothing for 20 seconds at a time. The second confuses transparency with error mapping - a provider 503 body is not an answer for the caller, and skipping validation turns a malformed body into a 200 - and the third changes where the loop runs, not how long it runs; each `await` already yields to the loop, so starvation is not the symptom. The fix is the shape the bank's skeleton uses: a bounded attempt count, a retryable status set, and a 504 after the last attempt.

mcqs.question: Your AI service is a README plus source: `uv sync`, `export MODEL_KEY=...`, `uvicorn app.main:app`. A reviewer opens the repo before the interview and finds nothing else. Which single artifact closes most of the gap those postings describe?
options: A Dockerfile with a pinned base image and lockfile that starts the service with the key read from the environment.
A compose stack that also runs Postgres and Redis, so the reviewer sees the whole system come up with one command.
A Kubernetes deployment behind a service, because a container that is not orchestrated is not deployable.
A Makefile that wraps install, run and test, so the reviewer gets the same commands you used instead of guessing.
mcqs.explanation: One container on a managed runtime is the bar the posting data describes: the Dockerfile proves the three things a README cannot - the same image runs somewhere else, the runtime and dependencies are pinned, and the key is configuration rather than code - which is what the ops pairing in 70.6% of AI-First postings is asking about. The strongest distractor is the Kubernetes option, because 'more infrastructure reads as more production-ready' is the reflex: the bank's answer says the opposite, that Kubernetes is a platform-team concern for most application-layer roles, and a manifest around an image nobody can start is decoration. Compose adds stateful services nobody asked for, turning a one-command review into a debugging session, and the Makefile only automates the commands that already worked on your machine, which is exactly the parity claim it leaves unproven.

mcqs.question: The posting data puts AWS at 40.3% of 6,964 AI postings, Azure at 29.6%, GCP at 27.4%, and pairs GenAI with ops in 70.6%. You can learn one platform properly this quarter. Which plan does that table support?
options: Kubernetes, because it runs on all three platforms and the ops pairing is the larger signal in the table.
One platform, AWS first as the most requested: 40.3% against 29.6% is a lead, and depth in one is what the table is asking for.
All three, because the shares are additive: 40.3 + 29.6 + 27.4 leaves only 2.7% of the postings uncovered by your plan.
None, because the 70.6% ops pairing is satisfied by Docker and a CI pipeline, with the platform left implicit.
mcqs.explanation: The three cloud figures are keyword mentions in a posting set, and nothing in the table makes them exclusive: a posting can name two clouds, so the table supports 'one cloud is expected, not all three', and the ordering follows the biggest share, AWS at 40.3%. The strongest distractor is the additive one, because the arithmetic looks like evidence and it is the classic misuse of a keyword table - summing non-exclusive shares manufactures coverage that was never measured. The Docker-or-nothing option reads ops and platform as the same requirement, but the platform is listed separately from the pairing, and the Kubernetes option swaps a platform skill for an orchestrator: it runs anywhere, which is precisely why it says nothing about the cloud the posting names.

mcqs.question: In Spain SQL appears in 23.3% of AI Engineer postings against 27.8% of general tech postings, the only skill in that study that goes down. A candidate drops joins and schema design from the plan because of it. Which correction is the defensible one?
options: The gap tracks the work: once vectors live in the index, schema design and access rules move into the vector database and SQL stops mattering.
The gap is a title artefact: AI Engineers never touch rows, because the analytics engineer owns every query the role depends on.
The gap is a keyword signal: schema, keys, freshness and access rules still decide what retrieval grounds on, so the work stays.
The gap means retrieval replaces modelling: if the answer is assembled from retrieved chunks, how the rows are shaped no longer affects it.
mcqs.explanation: SQL being mentioned less does not make the modelling go away: PostgreSQL is the default store in the field guide's stack, vector databases appear in about 1,647 of the 6,964 postings, and grounding an answer in company data begins with deciding what a row means - a schema decision before it is a retrieval one. The strongest distractor is the vector-index option, because pgvector makes 'the vectors live in the database' feel like a migration of everything: the bank's reading is the opposite, that keeping vectors next to the rows and their ACLs is usually the advantage of the relational store. The title option hands a whole discipline to another role on the strength of a keyword count, and the retrieval option assumes chunk quality is independent of how the data was modelled, when the chunk is built from rows someone shaped.

mcqs.question: This is the only test in the service: it stubs `ModelClient.complete` to return a valid JSON body, posts to `/answer`, and asserts `r.status_code == 200` plus byte-for-byte equality with that body. It passes, and a reviewer blocks the merge. Which change addresses the gap?
options: Point the same test at the real provider in CI, so the suite proves the integration instead of proving a stub.
Relax the assertion to `assert 'answer' in r.json()`, so a wording change from the model cannot break the build.
Mark the test `@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=3)`, so provider variance stops blocking merges on flaky days.
Add one test per failure path: timeout, 429/5xx, schema-invalid body, and a retry that succeeds on the second call.
mcqs.explanation: The stub and the fixture are fine; what is missing is the failure half of the contract, which is the gap the bank names as the most common one in take-home services: the happy path is tested and the service has never seen a 429. The strongest distractor is the live-provider option, because 'test the real thing' is a good instinct applied at the wrong layer - a live call makes CI depend on credentials, egress and provider variance, which is exactly the design that hangs the pipeline, and the integration proof belongs in a separate non-blocking contract job. Relaxing the assertion hides a broken contract instead of catching it, and the rerun marker retries the symptom: the model is already stubbed, so a rerun only buries a real failure.

mcqs.question: An image is built with `docker build --build-arg MODEL_KEY=$MODEL_KEY -t llm-svc .` from a Dockerfile whose only relevant lines are `ARG MODEL_KEY` then `ENV MODEL_KEY=$MODEL_KEY`, pushed to a private registry, and run elsewhere with no environment set. The service works. What is the defect and the fix?
options: The key is written into the image config, so anyone who can pull it reads it: inject it at run time, not at build time, and rotate this one.
The `ENV` line is the whole problem: dropping it keeps the value out, because a build argument only exists during the build.
The private registry is the boundary: with push access restricted to the team, a key in the image is as protected as a secret manager.
A rebuild fixes it: `docker build --no-cache` after the change leaves no copy of the value behind in the image.
mcqs.explanation: `ENV` writes the value into the image configuration, so it travels with the image to everyone who can pull it - and the run with no environment set proves where the service got the key. The fix is to remove the secret from the build entirely: read it at run time from the platform environment or a secret manager, and rotate the key that shipped, because deleting the line does not reach the copies already pulled. The strongest distractor is the `ENV`-only option: a build argument is not a secret channel either, it is a build-time input recorded in the build's metadata and in any step that consumes it, so the pattern still leaks once that line goes. The private-registry option trades a real boundary for an access-control assumption - one misconfigured pull policy, one backup, one `docker save` - and `--no-cache` rebuilds locally while the immutable layers already on the registry stay as they were.

mcqs.question: The backend phase ships in two variants: Python as the depth track and TypeScript as the second one. A friend calls that hedging. Which defence matches what the data says?
options: TypeScript is the requirement for AI roles that involve a UI, so a Python-only path fails the screen on every full-stack title.
Python carries the demand and the SDKs ship there first; TypeScript is the role's second language and a valid full-stack path, not a substitute.
The two are interchangeable: the model call is an HTTP request, so the language changes the syntax and nothing an interviewer can measure.
Python is being displaced in AI tooling, so TypeScript is the hedge against a decline the postings have already started to show.
mcqs.explanation: The two tracks answer different markets: Python appears in about 70.8% of the analysed postings and 78.8% of AI Engineer postings in Spain because the tooling is Python-first, while the field guide calls TypeScript the recommended path from a frontend background and a real second language for the role, not a replacement for depth. The strongest distractor is the interchangeability claim, because it is half true: the model call is an HTTP call in either language, but the gate is reading and modifying a service in that language, which is measurable and is exactly what a pair session exercises. The UI option turns a second track into a per-title requirement the postings do not state, and the decline option invents a trend the same dataset contradicts.

mcqs.question: This query is rejected with 'window functions are not allowed in WHERE' instead of returning three rows per customer: `SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders WHERE row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) <= 3`. What is the fix, and why?
options: Add the missing frame clause, `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which makes the window legal inside WHERE.
Move the predicate to HAVING, which runs after the window is computed, so the rank is available there.
Rank in a subquery or CTE and filter the ranked rows outside: windows are computed after WHERE and GROUP BY, so no WHERE can see them.
Cast the rank, `(row_number() OVER (...))::int <= 3`, because the error is a bigint against integer comparison.
mcqs.explanation: Clause order is the mechanism: WHERE runs before grouping, HAVING filters groups, and window functions are evaluated after both, one value per surviving row, so a predicate on the rank has to live in a query that selects the rank - a subquery or CTE - where the filter can also be pushed down by the planner. The strongest distractor is HAVING, because it genuinely runs after WHERE and GROUP BY, which makes 'after the window' sound right; it is not, and PostgreSQL rejects a window function in HAVING for the same reason it rejects it in WHERE. The frame clause defines which rows each value covers, and no frame makes the call legal in WHERE; the cast option invents a type error, since `row_number()` returns bigint and comparing it to 3 would be fine if the clause were allowed at all (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-window.html).

mcqs.question: A `/chat` route returns `StreamingResponse(token_stream(prompt), media_type="text/plain")`, and `token_stream` iterates the provider's stream and yields each delta. Users press Stop after a few tokens. What does the server still owe, beyond closing the browser's socket?
options: Propagate the teardown into the provider call and account for it in a `finally`: close the upstream stream, record the partial tokens with a `cancelled` outcome, and do not swallow the cancellation path.
Change `media_type` to `text/event-stream`: an SSE connection is closed by the browser, and that close is what stops the provider from generating.
Nothing — the client's `AbortController` aborts the fetch, and aborting a fetch cancels the corresponding upstream request on the provider side.
Add a watchdog task that polls how long the request has been open and kills the process after the timeout.
mcqs.explanation: The browser's abort closes the browser-to-server connection; the server learns about it as a disconnect (Starlette's `StreamingResponse` listens for `http.disconnect` and tears the response down), but the server-to-provider request is a separate connection that only stops if your code propagates the cancellation — keep the upstream `await` inside the generator, do not `shield` it, and use `finally` to close the stream and record partial usage. The strongest distractor is the second one: SSE is a payload framing decision (`event:`/`data:` lines), not a lifecycle mechanism — switching to `text/event-stream` changes how the client parses bytes, not whether the provider stops generating, because the disconnect signal already arrived either way. `AbortController` is necessary on the client and insufficient on the server, and a watchdog that kills the process is the heaviest possible way to save a socket.

mcqs.question: This batch runs `await asyncio.gather(*(ask(p) for p in prompts))`, where `ask` holds a `Semaphore(8)` and wraps the provider call in `asyncio.timeout(20)`. One prompt comes back `429`. Which description of what actually happens is correct?
options: The await raises the `429` immediately and the sibling tasks keep running — they are not cancelled — so their cost and side effects still happen; `return_exceptions=True` or a `TaskGroup` makes the failure policy explicit.
`gather` cancels every in-flight sibling before re-raising, which is what makes the batch fail fast instead of paying for the rest of the calls.
`gather` waits for every task to finish and then raises the first exception it observed, so no work is wasted.
The `429` is placed in the results list as an exception object and the successful answers are returned normally in their original positions.
mcqs.explanation: Per the asyncio docs, with the default `return_exceptions=False` the first raised exception is propagated to whoever awaits the `gather`, and the other awaitables in the sequence are *not* cancelled — they continue running, releasing the semaphore only when they finish or hit their own 20-second timeout. That is why the failure policy has to be chosen deliberately: `return_exceptions=True` collects outcomes, a `TaskGroup` cancels siblings on first error, and per-task try/except gives a per-prompt status. The strongest distractor is the second one: sibling cancellation on first failure is `TaskGroup` behaviour, and conflating the two is the usual reason a batch quietly keeps billing after the caller has already returned a 500.

mcqs.question: A service exposes a single probe, `/healthz`, which pings the model provider and the database and returns 503 if either takes longer than a second. During a 90-second provider incident the platform restarts every instance repeatedly and the service goes down. What is the correct fix?
options: Split the checks by meaning: liveness answers only "is this process alive" with no external calls; readiness answers "should this instance receive traffic" from local state. A provider blip then surfaces as latency and errors, not as a fleet-wide restart loop.
Raise `timeoutSeconds` on the probe and add retries, so a 90-second blip can never fail the check.
Keep the provider ping in `/healthz`, but cache the result for 60 seconds so a blip is averaged out instead of restarting the fleet.
Point the probe at the provider's public status page instead of calling the API, so the check stays cheap while still reflecting provider health.
mcqs.explanation: Liveness and readiness answer different questions, and only one of them is allowed to restart a process: a failing liveness probe kills and restarts the instance, so any external dependency in it turns a third-party incident into a self-inflicted outage (and gating readiness on a provider can remove every instance from rotation, which is the same outage wearing a different hat). The strongest distractor is the timeout bump: it is the reflex that looks like tuning but keeps the dependency in the restart path — a blip longer than the budget still restarts the fleet, and a generous timeout plus retries also delays the legitimate restart of a genuinely hung process. Caching and status-page polling both keep an external system in charge of the restart decision, just at a different latency.

scenarios.prompt: The take-home service is deployed to a preview URL and the reviewer left three notes in the first hour: the provider key is visible in the module source; /summarize hangs until the gateway cuts the request at 60 seconds whenever the provider stalls; and when the provider answers with an error body, the browser gets a 500 with a traceback. Review the endpoint and ship the version you would defend in the interview.
rubric: Names the committed key, says the value survives in git history and every clone, and requires rotation rather than only deleting the line.
Replaces `dict` in and `dict` out with a typed request and response contract, so a missing field is a 422 and the output shape is enforced.
Fixes the deadline and the failure mapping: explicit connect/read timeout, bounded retry on 429/5xx, and 502/504 with a typed body instead of a traceback.
Adds a test per failure path - timeout, provider error body, schema-invalid output, one retry that succeeds - rather than another happy-path test.
Pins the runtime and moves configuration to the environment so the deployed artifact is the one a reviewer can run.

scenarios.prompt: The same image and the same command pass in eight seconds on a laptop. In CI the job produces no failure at all: the log simply ends with the test that was running when the runner hit its 20-minute limit. The runner has no egress to the provider and no proxy variables; the laptop has both, plus MODEL_KEY exported in the shell. The only test in the repository posts to /answer and calls the real model client. Diagnose in order, then say what you would change in the test design, not only in the pipeline.

code.code:
# CI runs: docker build -t llm-svc . && docker run --rm llm-svc pytest -q
def test_answer(client):
    r = client.post("/answer", json={"question": "Can I return an item?"})
    assert r.status_code == 200

scenarios.modelAnswer:
The log already localises the problem: pytest started and one test was still running at the limit, so this is not a missing dependency or a broken image, it is a request that never finishes. Everything below is measurement, not guessing.

**1. Make the hang fail fast.** Run the same container with a suite timeout - `docker run --rm llm-svc pytest -q -x --timeout=10` with `pytest-timeout` - and the 20-minute silence becomes one red test in ten seconds. Without that, every later diagnosis is paid for in pipeline minutes.

**2. Separate the two candidate causes.** A blocked connect and a slow provider both look like "hangs" from outside; the traceback of the timed-out test separates them. A client with no deadline (or an SDK whose default is measured in minutes) will wait on a connect that is being dropped, and it will also retry internally, so the wall-clock time tells you almost nothing. Check reachability from the runner first - DNS resolution, then a connect to the provider's host - before reading any application code.

**3. Name the design bug the CI exposed.** A test that calls the real provider is not a unit test: it needs credentials, egress and provider availability, and it fails differently in three environments. That is the actual defect, and the pipeline only made it visible.

What I would change:

- **Inject the model client.** The answer path takes a client behind a small protocol (or FastAPI dependency override) that returns canned responses; the tests assert the contract - status, response schema, error mapping - not the provider's wording.
- **Keep one live contract test out of the blocking path.** A separate, non-blocking job (nightly, or manual) calls the real API with a real key and asserts the response shape, so integration is still covered where flakiness cannot block a merge.
- **Secrets at run time.** `docker run --env-file` or the platform's secret store, never a build argument or a layer; if the contract job needs the key, it is a CI secret, not a Dockerfile input.
- **Timeouts everywhere.** On the HTTP client and on the suite, so an environment fault is one red test in seconds instead of a runner at its limit.
- **Mirror the environment on purpose.** If CI must reach the provider, propagate `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` into the container explicitly; if it must not, the fake client is what turns that into a decision instead of an accident.
rubric: Reads the log to localise the hang (pytest started, one test was running) instead of assuming the image or the network, and adds a suite timeout so a hang fails in seconds.
Separates unreachable dependencies from slow ones with a measurement (DNS, then connect, then the timed-out traceback) before touching application code.
Names the real defect: a test that calls the live provider cannot be deterministic, and injects a fake model client for the blocking suite.
Keeps one live contract test outside the blocking pipeline so integration coverage does not disappear.
Keeps the key out of the build (runtime env or secret store) and propagates proxy configuration explicitly when CI must reach the provider.

scenarios.prompt: Product wants the assistant to remember users across sessions. A teammate ships this schema and this read path, and the first three support tickets are: after a replay the assistant answers its own previous message as if the user had written it; 'delete that message' is a request the team cannot fulfil; and the monthly cost report cannot attribute spend to a conversation. Review the storage design and give the schema and read path you would ship.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
The three tickets have one cause: the row is a user, not a message, so nothing in the table has an identity you can act on. No `role` means the replay cannot say who said what, which is the first ticket; no per-message key means "delete that message" is a rewrite of a blob, which is the second; no usage columns mean cost has no unit to attribute to, which is the third. The text column is the symptom, the model is the cause.

The shape that answers all three:

```sql
CREATE TABLE conversations (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  started_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE messages (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  conversation_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES conversations (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (role IN ('user', 'assistant', 'tool')),
  content TEXT NOT NULL,
  model TEXT,
  prompt_version TEXT,
  tokens_in INT,
  tokens_out INT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX messages_conversation_created_idx
  ON messages (conversation_id, created_at);
```

One row per message, ordered by `created_at` inside a conversation, with `role` carrying who spoke and the token columns carrying the cost. The index matches the only read that matters: the last N messages of one conversation.

The read path changes with it. Take the recent turns by a token budget rather than taking whatever fits, build the messages array from `role` and `content`, and summarise the dropped middle into a stored summary instead of truncating silently - that summary is part of what was sent, so version it. Storing `model` and `prompt_version` next to the rows is what makes a replay of an old answer explainable.

Deletion and retention become single statements instead of an edit of a blob: `DELETE FROM messages WHERE id = $1` for one message, `DELETE FROM messages WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days'` for the window, with the retention rule and the privacy decision written down rather than implied by the schema. Row-level access has to live in the same path: retrieval must filter on the same tenant or ACL the API checks, or the assistant becomes a way around the product's permissions.

Last, do not store what you do not need. If the product requires the exact input that produced an answer, store that input; chain-of-thought and raw provider payloads are a liability, not an audit trail.
rubric: Identifies the root cause as the row model: one row per user with no role, no message identity and no timestamp, so replay and deletion are guesses.
Models messages as rows with conversation, role, content and created_at, with an index that matches the read path.
Replaces 'read the whole column' with a bounded read (recent turns by token budget plus a stored summary) and keeps the summary reproducible.
Answers retention and privacy explicitly: per-message deletion, a retention window, and access rules that mirror what the API enforces.
Adds token and cost columns (plus model or prompt version) so spend and behaviour can be attributed to a conversation.

scenarios.prompt: This dashboard query became slow once orders passed a few million rows: p95 went from 300 ms to 3.8 s, and the page that calls it times out at 5 s. Say what you would change in the query and why, and how you would prove the change worked. You do not have the plan output yet, so name what you expect to find in it and in the measurement.

code.code:
SELECT o.id, c.name,
       (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders x WHERE x.customer_id = o.customer_id) AS total
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON UPPER(c.email) = UPPER(o.customer_email)
WHERE o.created_at::date = '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 50;

scenarios.modelAnswer:
Four changes, in the order I would make them, each with the measurement that proves it.

**1. The correlated subquery is the multiplier.** `(SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders x WHERE x.customer_id = o.customer_id)` runs once per row of `orders` that survives the filter, so the work scales with the day's order count, times that customer's order count. Aggregate once and join the result.

**2. The join and the filter both wrap the column in a function.** `UPPER(c.email) = UPPER(o.customer_email)` cannot use an index on `customers.email`, and `o.created_at::date = '2026-10-01'` cannot use one on `orders.created_at`; both force a scan of the big side. Normalise once - a stored lowercase column or an expression index - and compare a half-open range, `>= '2026-10-01' AND < '2026-10-02'`, which is index-friendly and correct at the boundary. The join itself goes through email while `orders` already carries `customer_id`: join on the id and keep email as an attribute, which also takes the case-folding question out of the hot path.

**3. `ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 50` sorts after the aggregation.** That becomes cheap once there is one row per order instead of one aggregation per order, but it is still a sort of everything that matched; the plan should show a top-N heapsort, not a spill to disk.

**4. The rewrite, with the semantics held fixed.** The total is over all of a customer's orders, not just that day's, so the aggregation cannot be pushed into the filtered set: a `SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)` computed after `WHERE` would sum only the surviving rows and silently change the number.

```sql
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT o.id, c.name, t.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN totals t    ON t.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-10-01'
  AND o.created_at <  '2026-10-02'
ORDER BY t.total DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

That still reads all of `orders` to build the totals. If the dashboard runs constantly, the honest next step is a maintained per-customer total - a materialised view or a rollup table - with a stated staleness, not a cleverer query.

**Proving it.** `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before and after, on the same data, read node by node. Expect to find, in the old plan: a `SubPlan` whose `loops` equals the rows the outer node emits (the subquery executing per row); `Seq Scan on orders` with millions of `Rows Removed by Filter` (the cast defeating `created_at`); and a hash join whose condition is on `upper(...)` (the function on the join key). In the new plan: an index range scan on `created_at`, no `SubPlan`, one aggregation node, and no spill. If an estimate is far from its actual row count, fix the statistics before rewriting the query again. The change is proven when those nodes are gone or small, the elapsed time is under the page timeout, and the estimates match the actuals.
rubric: Replaces the correlated subquery with one aggregation pass and keeps its semantics - the total covers all of a customer's orders, not only the filtered day.
Removes the functions that disable the indexes: `UPPER` on the join key and `::date` on the filter, replaced by normalised data and a half-open range.
Notices that the join goes through email while `orders` already has `customer_id`, and joins on the id instead.
Names what the plan should show before and after - `SubPlan` loops, `Rows Removed by Filter`, estimate versus actual - and re-measures to prove the change.
States the residual cost (the totals still read all of `orders`) and the trade-off it accepts, instead of claiming the query is now free.

scenarios.prompt: This endpoint streams model output to the browser. Review it as a senior engineer: name the failure modes you would block a merge on, then describe the contract you would ship instead — including what the server, the provider call and the accounting each do when the user cancels mid-answer or the provider fails after the first token.

code.code:
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()
PROVIDER_URL = "https://api.provider.example/v1/chat"
client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=None)


async def token_stream(prompt: str):
    parts: list[str] = []
    async with client.stream(
        "POST", PROVIDER_URL, json={"prompt": prompt, "stream": True}
    ) as resp:
        async for chunk in resp.aiter_bytes():
            text = chunk.decode("utf-8")
            parts.append(text)
            yield text
    await usage.record(prompt=prompt, completion="".join(parts), outcome="ok")


@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(body: ChatRequest):
    return StreamingResponse(token_stream(body.prompt), media_type="text/plain")

scenarios.modelAnswer:
Start by separating three things the code conflates: the transport (one HTTP response), the framing (where one event ends and the next begins) and the lifecycle (who stops what when the user leaves).

Blocking issues, in the order I would raise them:

1. **No deadline.** `AsyncClient(timeout=None)` means a provider that accepts the connection and then stalls holds the request, the connection and a worker slot forever — no error, no metric, just a socket that never resolves. Set an explicit `httpx.Timeout(connect=..., read=..., write=..., pool=...)`, and note that a per-read timeout is not a total budget: if the answer may run long, add an overall `asyncio.timeout` and decide what a truncated answer looks like.
2. **`.decode()` on arbitrary byte chunks.** `aiter_bytes()` yields whatever the socket produced; a multi-byte UTF-8 character split across two chunks raises `UnicodeDecodeError` (or produces mojibake) — and this is the same category of error as assuming one chunk is one token. Use `resp.aiter_text()`, which decodes incrementally, or keep an incremental decoder.
3. **No framing.** Chunk boundaries are not message boundaries; the client cannot tell where a token ends, cannot distinguish a token from an error, and cannot tell a completed answer from a truncated one. Use SSE (`event: token`, `event: done`, `event: error` with `data:` payloads) or NDJSON with explicit delimiters, and document it.
4. **The 200 is already sent.** If the provider fails after the first byte you cannot return a 502; the honest contract is an in-band `event: error` followed by the end of the stream, and a client rule that a stream without `event: done` is a failed answer. Silently ending the body is the bug that shows up as "the answer just stops" in support tickets.
5. **Accounting only after the loop.** `usage.record` never runs on disconnect or on an upstream error, so exactly the requests you most want to measure — cancelled and failed ones — are the ones missing from cost data. Put the record in `finally`, include partial token counts and an outcome (`ok` / `cancelled` / `error`).
6. **Cancellation has to reach the provider.** Keep the upstream `await` inside the generator and do not `shield` it; when the response is torn down, the stream must close so the provider stops generating and stops billing. Note that `asyncio.CancelledError` is a `BaseException`, so a broad `except Exception` will not catch it — good, as long as nothing else swallows it. Keep that cleanup path short too: a slow write in `finally` delays the teardown for every cancelled request, so anything that can block belongs on a queue.
7. **Buffering in front of you.** Compression middleware or a reverse proxy can hold the body until it is large enough, which turns the stream back into a single response in production only. Disable compression for this route, send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` and `Cache-Control: no-cache`, and verify the first byte arrives before completion with a real request, not a unit test.
8. **Client lifecycle.** A module-level `AsyncClient` is the right call for connection pooling, but it must be closed in a lifespan shutdown hook — otherwise every deploy leaks connections and tests hang.

A version that keeps the contract explicit:

```python
import asyncio
import json
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse


async def token_stream(prompt: str, request: Request) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    sent = 0
    outcome = "cancelled"
    try:
        async with client.stream(
            "POST",
            PROVIDER_URL,
            json={"prompt": prompt, "stream": True},
            timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=5.0, read=30.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0),
        ) as resp:
            resp.raise_for_status()
            async for text in resp.aiter_text():      # incremental UTF-8 decode
                if await request.is_disconnected():
                    break
                sent += len(text)
                yield f"event: token\ndata: {json.dumps({'t': text})}\n\n"
        outcome = "ok"
        yield "event: done\ndata: {}\n\n"
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        raise                                          # let the server tear down
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        outcome = "error"
        yield 'event: error\ndata: {"message": "upstream failed"}\n\n'
    finally:
        await usage.record(prompt=prompt, chars=sent, outcome=outcome)


@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(body: ChatRequest, request: Request):
    return StreamingResponse(
        token_stream(body.prompt, request),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"},
    )
```

The tests that prove it: a fake provider that emits a multi-byte character split across chunks (no crash, no mojibake), a provider that 500s after the third token (client sees `event: error`, usage recorded as `error`), a client that disconnects mid-stream (upstream request closed, usage recorded as `cancelled`), and a slow first token with a proxy in front (the first byte is observed before the answer completes). FastAPI's stream-data and SSE docs plus MDN's readable-streams page describe the mechanics: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/stream-data/ , https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/ , https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Streams_API/Using_readable_streams
rubric: Separates transport, framing and lifecycle: treats chunk boundaries as unrelated to token boundaries and decodes incrementally instead of calling `.decode()` per chunk.
Propagates cancellation to the provider call and records partial usage in `finally`, with explicit `ok`/`cancelled`/`error` outcomes rather than a success-only path.
Defines a stream contract that survives the already-sent 200: framed events plus a terminal `done`/`error` event, and a client rule for truncated streams.
Sets a real deadline (connect/read timeouts, total budget for long answers) and knows proxy or compression buffering must be disabled and verified with a live request.
Backs the design with failure-path tests — disconnect, mid-stream provider error, split multi-byte character, slow first token — instead of only a happy-path test.
